questions.q: ___ is the decrease in the response that an organism gives to a stimulus to which it is exposed in numerous trials or occasions.
questions.explanation: Habituation = decreasing response with repeated exposure (wall-clock example); matches lecture and standard definition. (Lecture 5)

questions.q: Cooperative learning is shaped by three crucial elements. Which of the following is one of them?
questions.explanation: "Cooperative learning is primarily shaped by three crucial elements": heterogeneous groups, (positive interdependence), individual responsibility, so all of the given. (Lecture 5)

questions.q: Which of the following psychologists is an important contributor to the concept of observational learning?
questions.explanation: Observational learning is Bandura's social learning theory (lecture 7 covers attention-retention-production-motivation).

questions.q: Which of the following is not considered a pioneer of the behaviorism school of thought in psychology?
questions.explanation: "JB Watson, BF Skinner, Ivan Pavlov ... these are the pioneers of behaviorism"; Freud was a psychoanalyst. (Lecture 6: Major Theories of Learning)

questions.q: ___ is known as the father of modern psychology.
questions.explanation: Standard: Wundt is called the father of modern (experimental) psychology.

questions.q: Cognitivists objected to behaviorists because they felt that behaviorists ignored the important role of ___.
questions.explanation: Cognitivists rejected behaviourism for explaining behaviour only as S-R links and ignoring internal mental processes (thinking). (Lecture 7)

questions.q: ___ is viewed as the mainstream for all research on learning designs.
questions.explanation: Cognitivism is presented as the dominant approach for learning research and instructional design; other options do not fit. (Lecture 7)

questions.q: ___ is a perspective in psychology focusing on the belief that human consciousness cannot be broken down into its elements and is based on the concept of a 'whole'.
questions.explanation: Gestalt: "whole is more meaningful than the sum of its parts". (Lecture 7)

questions.q: Theory of multiple intelligences is given by
questions.explanation: Gardner's multiple intelligences (intrapersonal, interpersonal, logical-mathematical, musical ...). (Lecture 8)

questions.q: The general intelligence factor, also known as g, is what intelligence tests typically measure and refers only to ___ intelligence.
questions.explanation: Sternberg: g (general/academic intelligence) covers only academic/analytical ability. (Lecture 8)

questions.q: Cognitive evaluation for planning, attention, simultaneous, and successive processing of individuals can be done through CAS based on PASS theory. CAS here stands for ___.
questions.explanation: "they have developed the scale cognitive assessment system" based on PASS. (Lecture 9)

questions.q: BBL is a new science that shapes the learning process and is an approach that is based on the structure and function of the human brain. BBL stands for ___.
questions.explanation: "brain based learning ... the concept of learning in a neurophysiological context". (Lecture 9)

questions.q: Gagne's Conditions of Learning is also known as ___ Events of Instruction.
questions.explanation: Gagne "nine events ... provides a framework for designing and delivering the instruction". (Lecture 10)

questions.q: Which of the following is not a type of constructivism?
questions.explanation: Types named: cognitive (Piaget), social (Vygotsky), radical (von Glasersfeld); no biological constructivism. (Lecture 10)

questions.q: Which of the following is not one of the three major processes involved in memory?
questions.explanation: Three basic processes: encoding, storage, retrieval. (Lecture 11: Memory & Cognition)

questions.q: ___ refers to changing information into a usable form.
questions.explanation: "information must be changed to a usable form which occurs through a process known as encoding". (Lecture 11: Memory & Cognition)

questions.q: ___ refers to a range of mental processes relating to the acquisition, storage, manipulation and retrieval of information.
questions.explanation: "cognition refers to the range of mental processes starting from acquisition to storage to manipulation to retrieval". (Lecture 11: Memory & Cognition)

questions.q: Which of the following is a challenge faced by people with social cognition deficits?
options: difficulty in getting good academic scores
questions.explanation: Social cognition is a domain of cognition in the lecture; deficits = difficulty reading facial expressions (standard description). (Lecture 11: Memory & Cognition)

questions.q: Which of the following is not true about the assumptions underlying the Information Processing View of Learning?
options: Information processing is analogous to computer processing
The human information processing system is interactive
There is no limit on how much information can be processed at each stage
questions.explanation: Assumptions: processed in stages, "there are limits on how much information can be processed at each stage", interactive, analogous to computer. (Lecture 11: Memory & Cognition)

questions.q: ___ prevents the quick disappearance from short term memory of information
questions.explanation: "rehearsal prevents the quick disappearance of the information from short term memory" (Lecture 12)

questions.q: The Multicomponent Model of Working Memory is largely attributed to the work by
questions.explanation: Multicomponent working memory model (episodic buffer, phonological loop, sketchpad) = Baddeley. (Lecture 13)

questions.q: ___ memory refers to the events that can be reported from a person's life.
questions.explanation: Episodic memory = life events that can be reported (autobiographical episodes). (Lecture 14)

questions.q: The memory capacity depends on which of the following?
options: spatial and temporal correlations between memories
questions.explanation: Neural network model: capacity "depends on the complexity of the synapses, the sparseness of the representation, the spatial and temporal [correlations]" (and retrieval mode), so all. (Lecture 14)

questions.q: Which of the following is not one of the three measurable dimensions of cognitive load?
questions.explanation: "mental load, mental effort and the performances [are] the three measurable dimensions of cognitive load". (Lecture 15)

questions.q: The three main types of thinking in psychology include the following except
questions.explanation: "primary types of thinking ... creative thinking, divergent thinking, symbolic thinking"; convergent is the exception. (Lecture 16: Thinking & Cognition)

questions.q: Young children engaging in imaginative play often engage in ___ thinking.
questions.explanation: Imaginative play (playing roles like father, caretaker) is symbolic thinking. (Lecture 16: Thinking & Cognition)

questions.q: Which of the following is a way in which we think?
questions.explanation: "thinking also takes place in terms of mathematical symbols, in terms of gestures", and verbal symbols. (Lecture 16: Thinking & Cognition)

questions.q: People experience the ___ experience when they find the solution to a problem suddenly that had been in their mind for hours or days, late.
questions.explanation: Sudden solution after incubation = "Eureka moment"/aha experience (insight). (Lecture 19)

questions.q: ___ knowledge refers to knowledge of terminology and specific details.
questions.explanation: "factual knowledge ... relates to specific details, information, data" (terminology and details). (Lecture 17)

questions.q: Which of the following is not true about metacognition?
options: allows people to be dependent on others for their learning
often referred to as "thinking about thinking"
is crucial for efficient independent learning because it fosters self-reflection
is a regulatory system that helps a person understand and control his or her own cognitive performance
questions.explanation: Metacognition builds self-regulation and makes the learner independent; dependence on others is not true. (Lecture 18)

questions.q: Which of the following is not an effective way to develop reflective thinking?
questions.explanation: Ways listed: self-checking questions, asking questions, "joining reflective discussion", negotiated learning; avoiding discussion is not one. (Lecture 19)

questions.q: Which of the following is not true about creative thinking?
options: It is the ability to consider something in a new way
It is not a skill anybody can develop
It is the process of nurturing our imagination
It is all about developing innovative solutions to problems.
It requires a compilation of analytical, problem-solving, organizational and communication skills
questions.explanation: Lecture gives strategies to enhance creative thinking (puzzles, questioning, travel), so it can be developed. (Lecture 19)

questions.q: The ___ stage of the creative thinking process refers to the "eureka" moment.
questions.explanation: "all of a sudden that Eureka moment ... that is the Insight". (Lecture 19)

questions.q: In a concept map, two nodes connected with a labeled arrow are called a
questions.explanation: "the two nodes when they are connected they are called a proposition". (Lecture 20)

questions.q: Which of the following is not a causal factor for extrinsic motivation?
questions.explanation: L21: extrinsic causal factors 'lie in the external environment like reward, social pressure, punishment, financial gain'; curiosity is intrinsic.

questions.q: ___ refers to realizing the value of developing a skill/behavior.
questions.explanation: L21: 'identified regulation is that he is now realizing the whole value of developing that particular skill'.

questions.q: Drive theory is a psychological concept that attempts to explain why and how people behave in the ways they do. It is given by
questions.explanation: L22 slide: drive theory 'was created by behaviorist Clark Hull in 1943'.

questions.q: ___ theory that suggests that people are motivated to take action in order to receive a reward and is based on the idea of operant conditioning.
questions.explanation: L22 slide: 'Incentive theory... suggests that people are motivated to take action in order to receive a reward... based on operant conditioning'.

questions.q: The Yerkes Dodson law gives ___ relationship between arousal and performance.
questions.explanation: L22: Yerkes-Dodson curve - performance rises with arousal to an optimum then is impaired by excess arousal (inverted U).

questions.q: The expectancy theory is based on the assumption that ___.
options: our behavior is based on making a conscious choice from a set of possible alternative behaviors
individuals are motivated to seek out stimulation when they have low levels of arousal, but will become bored and unmotivated when they become too highly aroused
biological needs produce unpleasant states of arousal which people seek to reduce
questions.explanation: L22 slide: expectancy theory 'is based on the assumption that our behavior is based on making a conscious choice from a set of possible alternative behaviors'.

questions.q: Valence, or the perceived value of reward, would have ___ value if one wants to avoid that reward.
questions.explanation: L23: valence is the perceived value of the reward; 'it could be negative, it could be zero...' - negative when one wants to avoid it (Vroom).

questions.q: Which of the following is not true about Maslow's need hierarchy?
options: Needs lower down in the hierarchy must be satisfied before individuals can attend to higher needs
Safety needs lie at the bottom of the pyramid
Deficiency needs are concerned with basic survival a
Growth needs are more psychological needs
Motivation is seen as being not just concerned with tension reduction and survival but also with human growth and development
questions.explanation: L24: base of the pyramid is physiological needs (food, water, warmth), safety is second, so 'safety needs at the bottom' is false.

questions.q: Self-Determination Theory differentiates between ___ and ___ motivation types.
questions.explanation: L24: 'self determination theory differentiates between the autonomous motivation and control(led) motivation'.

questions.q: In achievement motivation, the motive to avoid failure often consists of
options: worries about the consequences of failing
questions.explanation: L25 slide: 'motive to avoid failure includes worries about the consequences of failing, self-criticism, ... accelerated heart rate'.

questions.q: Daniel Goleman's work in emotional intelligence (EI) has outlined ___ main areas of this intelligence.
questions.explanation: L26 slide: 'Daniel Goleman's work in emotional intelligence has outlined five main areas'.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is not true?
options: Experts even suggested that emotional intelligence/ EQ, is more important than IQ/academic intelligence
An individual with high EI is not only aware of what emotions they are feeling but can put words to their feelings
Studies show that EI does not impact aspects of one's life like academic performance
Peter Salovey and John Mayer were the first to develop a psychological theory of emotional intelligence.
questions.explanation: L26: 'emotional intelligence can... positively impact their academic performance', so the 'does not impact' statement is false.

questions.q: ___ refers to how tuned to the emotions of others a person is.
questions.explanation: L26: empathy is 'how tuned to the emotion of others a person is'.

questions.q: The following are advantages of developing emotional intelligence, except------
options: Being able to accept criticism and responsibility
Knowing why we do the things we do
Being able to say no when we need to
Being able to hide our feelings from others
questions.explanation: L27 slide 'Advantages of Developing EI' lists accepting criticism, saying no, knowing why we do things, sharing (not hiding) feelings.

questions.q: The Pyramid of Emotional Intelligence is also known as the ___ layer model.
questions.explanation: L27: 'it is nine layer pyramid through which we can understand how emotional intelligence develops'.

questions.q: EI can be developed at any stage of life through self-effort & training.
questions.explanation: L28 slide: 'EI can be developed at any stage of life through self-effort & training'.

questions.q: When someone engages in ___, they can regulate their emotions to ensure that others feel more comfortable.
questions.explanation: L29: emotional labor = managing/displaying emotions as the job demands to make others (passengers, customers) feel good.

questions.q: The management of emotions is ___
options: influenced by cultural and social norms
done by actively shaping and directing feelings
questions.explanation: L29: management of emotion 'is essentially a private act' yet culture-specific, shaped by social norms of what is appropriate to feel; all apply.

questions.q: ___ is seen when workers change their outward emotional expressions but do not attempt to feel the emotions that they are displaying.
questions.explanation: L29: surface acting 'is when the workers change their outward emotional expression but do not attempt to feel the emotion that they are displaying'.

questions.q: The concept of emotional contagion can be linked to biological basis of ___
questions.explanation: L29: emotional contagion explained by mirror neurons in the cortex.

questions.q: ___ defined learning as 'a change in human disposition or capacity that persists over a period of time and is not simply ascribable to processes of growth.'
questions.explanation: L31: 'Robert Gagne defined learning as a change in human disposition or capacity that persists over a period of time and is not simply ascribable to processes of growth'.

questions.q: The principles of contiguity (how close in time two events must be for a bond to be formed) and reinforcement (any means of increasing the likelihood that an event will be repeated) are central to explaining the learning process in the ___ orientation to learning.
questions.explanation: L31: in behaviorist orientation 'this principle of contiguity and reinforcement these are the primary factors that explain the learning process'.

questions.q: Which of the following is not true about humanistic orientations to learning?
options: It has a quality of personal involvement
The locus of evaluation resides definitely outside the learner
questions.explanation: L31: humanistic learning - personal involvement, self-initiated, pervasive; 'locus of evaluation... resides within the learner'.

questions.q: The concept of situated learning is studied under which school of thought of learning theories?
questions.explanation: L32: situated learning discussed under the social & situational orientation (co-participation, communities of practice).

questions.q: Which of the following is not one of the individual variable factors affecting learning?
questions.explanation: L32: individual variables = interest, perception, past experience, learning capabilities, endurance, ego; ergonomics is an environmental variable.

questions.q: ___ learners prefer maps, graphs, diagrams and charts to learn.
questions.explanation: L32: visual learners learn through 'maps, graphs, diagrams, charts, visual aids'.

questions.q: ___ learners search for connections, causes, patterns, and results in their learning.
questions.explanation: L32: logical/analytical learners look for 'the connection between the concepts, causes, factors, the patterns'.

questions.q: Effective instruction is ___
options: designed to accommodate student learning needs and styles
questions.explanation: L33: effective instruction is interactive, eclectic, generative and dynamic, accommodates learner needs, uses pedagogical approaches - all of the given.

questions.q: ___ role of the trainer consists of transmitting information about a subject to the audience.
questions.explanation: L33: 'the role of the trainer... he's an expert... because he transmits the information about the subject to the audience'.

questions.q: Which of the following is not a component of the ADDIE model?
questions.explanation: L33: ADDIE = analysis, design, development, implementation, evaluation; integration not a component.

questions.q: The word 'pedagogy' has been derived from the Greek word "pedagogue" which stands for
questions.explanation: L36: 'it has come from the Greek word... pedagogue means the art of teaching the children'.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is not true about pedagogy?
options: It assists both students and teachers in gaining an in-depth understanding of fundamental material.
It is about suppressing responses from learners
It enables teachers to influence student learning with an intention to capture the attention of students
questions.explanation: L36: good pedagogy aims 'to elicit the responses that demonstrate understanding', not to suppress them.

questions.q: Which of the following is not a pedagogical approach in teaching?
questions.explanation: L36 slide: five approaches - constructivist, collaborative, inquiry-based, integrative, reflective; 'collective' is not one.

questions.q: ___ is a form of active learning that starts by posing questions, problems or scenarios rather than simply presenting established facts or portraying a smooth path to knowledge.
questions.explanation: L36: inquiry-based approach 'is a form of active learning... posing questions, problems'.

questions.q: Which of the following is a primary role of the instructor in experiential learning?
questions.explanation: L37 slide: 'instructor's primary roles include setting suitable experiences, posing problems, setting boundaries, supporting students...'.

questions.q: The "what is important?" stage of the experiential learning process refers to the ___ stage
questions.explanation: L37 slide: 'Processing/Analyzing "What's Important?"'.

questions.q: The ___ learning style as given by Kolb suggests that these individuals prefer to look at things from multiple perspectives and prefer to watch rather than do.
questions.explanation: L37: diverging style - 'look at things from multiple perspectives... prefer to watch rather than do'.

questions.q: The following factors influence preferred learning style except
questions.explanation: L37: factors influencing learning style - adaptive competencies, career choice, current job role, educational specialization, personality type; not genes.

questions.q: Integrative learning often involves three steps. Which of the following is not one of them?
questions.explanation: L37: integrative learning 'involves these three steps... integrative inquiry, application and transfer, and then reflection'.

questions.q: In transformative learning, ___ includes a student's habit of the mind, as well as a personal point of view.
questions.explanation: L39: 'a frame of reference includes... a student's habit of mind as well as the personal point of view'.

questions.q: E-learning implies ___ learning.
questions.explanation: L41: 'e-learning is the very comprehensive term which implies the computer enhanced learning, technology enhanced learning'.

questions.q: ___ type of e-learning is highly interactive, which includes graphics, video, audio and games too.
questions.explanation: L41 slide: 'Simulation: It is a highly interactive kind of e-learning, which includes graphics, video, audio and games too.'

questions.q: Which of the following is not true about e-learning?
options: one can have access to the content any number of times
it helps in developing new policies
it saves time for the students, they don't need to travel to the institution
it is targeted to cater to the needs of students specifically
questions.explanation: L41 slide benefits: accommodates everyone's needs (working person, housewife or student), lectures can be taken multiple times/'access the content any number of times', scalability 'facilitates in developing and communicating new training policies' - so d (targeted specifically at students) is not true.

questions.q: As learning depends on the learner's prior experience, and no two learners will have the same experiences, new information will be dealt with in different ways by different learners. This statement means that learning is
questions.explanation: L42: 'learning is very peculiar, very idiosyncratic ... as the learning depends on learners prior experience'.

questions.q: Which of the following is a way of facilitating the social dimension to learning?
questions.explanation: L41/L42: social dimension via discussion forums, emails/instant messages, blogs, virtual communities of practice - all of these.

questions.q: We can say that when we're good at something after practice, it's usually because
options: our brain has released better chemicals
our brain has made stronger connections with this information
our brain has prioritized this information over others
questions.explanation: L42 slide: 'when we're good at something, it's usually because our brain has made stronger connections with this information'.

questions.q: Learners may multitask when engaging in an online course, which could be resulting in
questions.explanation: L43: continuous multitasking 'makes our attention span very short'.

questions.q: The cognitive load theory suggests that when we overload our ___ we are unable to acquire and process new information.
questions.explanation: L43: working memory has limited capacity; continuous e-learning overloads it creating cognitive load.

questions.q: There are five critical aspects of psychology which are needed to guarantee the implementation of successful eLearning. Which of the following is not one of them?
questions.explanation: L43: five critical aspects - motivation, emotion, self-discipline, social skills, stress; evolution is not one.

questions.q: ___ is a learning tool, because the explicit navigation of the topic and association types might enable meaningful learning and it helps to reduce the cognitive loads caused by E-learning content and constant attention.
questions.explanation: L43: 'topic map ... is a tool and explicit navigation ... enables the meaningful learning ... reduces cognitive load'.

questions.q: The Readiness Model for New Normal in Education designed by many educational institutions caters to the following components except
questions.explanation: L46 slides: Readiness Model for New Normal - Parents' Readiness, Teachers' Readiness, Learners' Readiness; no society readiness.

questions.q: In 2018, Global Education and Skills Forum noted that the 'future' teacher would need some skills to thrive in the 21st century. Which of the following is not one of them?
questions.explanation: L46 slide (GESF 2018) skills: strong subject knowledge, being a facilitator, strong social skills, external focus, data analysis; 'internal focus' is not one.

questions.q: Which of the following impacts student learning?
options: Their perception about their intelligence and ability
questions.explanation: L46 principles: self-perception of intelligence/ability, prior knowledge, and context all affect learning.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is not true?
options: Techniques linked to self-control contribute to more effective learning if taught and applied correctly
Clear, explanatory and timely feedback to students is important for learning
Students tend to enjoy learning and have better outcomes when their motivation is more extrinsic than intrinsic
questions.explanation: L47 principle 9: students enjoy learning and do better 'when their motivation is more intrinsic than extrinsic' - option d reverses it.

questions.q: Both formative and summative assessment are important and useful, provided they are applied and interpreted appropriately.
questions.explanation: L47/L49: formative and summative assessment are both important and useful, complementary.

questions.q: Individual differences are the unique ways each human being differs from another. It can be handled through using different techniques. Which of the following is not one of them?
questions.explanation: L48 slide: individual differences handled through 'observation, interviews, rating scales', sociograms etc.; ignorance is not a technique.

questions.q: Clapping is an example of ___ reward.
questions.explanation: L48 slide: 'A reward may be social, such as clapping, or tangible, such as giving...'.

questions.q: ___ is the process of judging the value or worth of an individual's achievements or characteristics.
questions.explanation: L49: 'evaluation is the process for verifying, valuing or judging the worth of an individual's achievements and/or characteristics'.

questions.q: ___ refers to the frequent, interactive assessment of student progress to identify learning needs and shape teaching.
questions.explanation: L49: formative assessment is frequent, intermittent assessment to map progress, give feedback and modify teaching.

questions.q: "That is an intelligent response, well done" is an example of a ___ level feedback.
questions.explanation: L50 slide: '3: Personal-level feedback ... directed to the self ... Example: That's an intelligent response, well done.'

questions.q: ___ refers to a complex set of mental abilities underlying social stimulus perception, processing, interpretation, and response.
questions.explanation: L51: 'social cognition ... refers to a complex set of mental abilities underlying social stimulus perception, processing, interpretation and response'.

questions.q: Piaget's conception of ___ views information inconsistent with an individual's cognitive structures as an initiator for assimilation and accommodation processes.
questions.explanation: L54 slide: 'Piaget's conception of cognitive conflict views information' inconsistent with cognitive structures as initiator of assimilation/accommodation.

questions.q: During the earliest stages of development, children see the world from their own perspective and struggle to think about how other people may view the world. This highlights that initially, children are
questions.explanation: L51: 'at the young stage every child is very much egocentric'.

questions.q: Which of the following is false regarding social cognition?
options: It develops in childhood and adolescence
When looking at a social situation, any two people may have wildly different interpretations.
It includes complex abilities like theory of mind
There are no cultural differences in social cognition
questions.explanation: L51/L52: social cognition develops in childhood and adolescence, two people may interpret wildly differently, includes theory of mind, and 'there are cultural differences in social cognition'.

questions.q: Social processes influence how information is selected, organized, integrated, and retrieved. This highlights the ___ hypothesis.
questions.explanation: L54: 'cognitive influence hypothesis ... social processes influence how the information is selected, organized, integrated and retrieved'.

questions.q: The social cognitive theory is developed by ___.
questions.explanation: L52: 'social cognitive theory is actually a learning theory developed by Albert Bandura'.

questions.q: ___ refers to the internal or external responses to a person's behavior that affect the likelihood of continuing or discontinuing the behavior.
questions.explanation: L53: reinforcement 'refers to the internal and external responses ... that affects the likelihood of continuing ... or discontinuing' the behaviour.

questions.q: Observational learning occurs through the sequence of ___ number of processes. One of those is attentional processes.
questions.explanation: L53: 'observational learning occur through a sequence of the four processes' - attentional, retention, production, motivational.

questions.q: The ___ model of observational learning involves an actual individual demonstrating or acting out a behavior.
questions.explanation: L53: Bandura's three models - live model (actual individual demonstrating behaviour), symbolic, verbal instructional.

questions.q: ___ suggests that our behavior, personal factors, and environmental factors all influence each other.
questions.explanation: L53: 'reciprocal determinism ... our behavior, personal factor, environmental factors all influence each other'.

questions.q: Sustainable development is
questions.explanation: L56 slide (Eggert 2009): 'Sustainable development is multidimensional as it integrates...'.

questions.q: Revenue generation and resource use are components of
questions.explanation: L56: economic sustainability relates to 'revenue generation, alternative uses of resources, resource monitoring ... resource use'.

questions.q: ___ as a practice is defined as solving social problems using market based methods and can create both economic and social value.
questions.explanation: L56 slide: 'Social entrepreneurship, defined as solving social problems using market-based methods' creating economic and social value.

questions.q: In the context of sustainability, HESI highlights the role of ___ in building a better world for current and future generations.
questions.explanation: L57: HESI 'highlights the role of higher education and higher education institutions in building a better world for current and future generations'.

questions.q: The following are the outcome targets of SDG 4, except.
questions.explanation: L57 SDG 4 outcome targets: universal primary/secondary, early childhood, equal access to TVET/higher ed, relevant skills for decent work, gender equality and inclusion, universal youth literacy, citizenship/ESD; no privatization.

questions.q: One of the means to implement SDG 4 is exponentially increasing the number of scholarships available to developing contexts.
questions.explanation: L57 slide: '4.b Scholarships - By 2030, substantially expand globally the number of scholarships available to developing countries'. 'Exponentially' is probably a paraphrase (True), but the changed word could be an intended falsification.

questions.q: Successful implementation of ESD requires a shift in focus from
questions.explanation: L58 slide: 'Successful implementation of ESD requires a shift in focus from teaching to learning and a multidisciplinary approach'.

questions.q: ___ refers to the ability to understand and evaluate multiple possible futures to deal with risks and changes.
questions.explanation: L58/L59: anticipatory competency - 'ability to understand and evaluate multiple futures ... to deal with the risk and changes'.

questions.q: Fostering competencies requires integration of three interrelated dimensions of learning as described by UNESCO. Which of the following is not one of them?
questions.explanation: L58 slide: three interrelated dimensions of learning (UNESCO) - cognitive, social and emotional, behavioral; biological is not one.

questions.q: GAP in the context of Education for Sustainable Development stands for
questions.explanation: L59 slide: 'Global Action Programme (GAP) on ESD states that...'.

questions.q: Psychologists agree that learning results from ___
questions.explanation: "learning causes relatively permanent change in the behavior that results from the experience" (Lecture 1: Psychology of Learning)

questions.q: Learning is defined as a ___ change in behavior
questions.explanation: "learning brings a relatively permanent change in our behavior that results from experience" (Lecture 1: Psychology of Learning)

questions.q: ___ definitions of learning refer to a specific change in mental constructs (e.g., knowledge, representations, associations) of an organism.
questions.explanation: "the cognitive definition of learning ... refer to the specific change in the organism ... change in the mental constructs" (Lecture 1: Psychology of Learning)

questions.q: Who among the following was one of the first psychologists to study how learning influences behavior?
questions.explanation: Lecture presents John B. Watson as founder of behaviourism who studied learning and behaviour (Little Albert); others listed are not learning researchers. (Lecture 2: Psychology of Learning (Contd.))

questions.q: Which of the following is not an outcome of effective learning?
options: more developed vision of future self as a learner
questions.explanation: Effective learning outcomes listed: "more connected knowledge", "wider range of strategies", reflective approach, positive emotions; sad/anxious feelings is not one. (Lecture 3)

questions.q: Learning that consists of adding to existing student knowledge is known as
questions.explanation: "adding to the existing student knowledge known as the conceptual growth or the transforming or revising ... known as the conceptual change" (Lecture 3)

questions.q: What type of feedback to students is important for increasing learning?
questions.explanation: "clear explanatory And Timely feedback to student is important for learning" (Lecture 4)

questions.q: Getting used to of something like the ticking of a wall clock is an example of
questions.explanation: Habituation explained with the example "clicking of the wall clock ... as we become habituated to that then we overlook it". (Lecture 5)

questions.q: In ___ learning, special emphasis is placed on exchanges of information as a way of enriching work and the confluence of ideas
questions.explanation: Cooperative learning: "it is also exchange of information it is also enriching our work with the confluence of ideas". (Lecture 5)

questions.q: ___ is the process of gradually changing the quality of a response.
questions.explanation: "shaping is the process of gradually changing the quality of response" (Lecture 6: Major Theories of Learning)

questions.q: ___ established the first psychological laboratory at the University of Leipzig in Germany.
questions.explanation: Standard fact: Wundt opened the first psychology laboratory at Leipzig in 1879 (name not found in the captions).

questions.q: ___ is a theory of learning that uses mind as an information processor, like a computer
questions.explanation: "just like the computer mind is an information processor" in the cognitive school (cognitivism). (Lecture 7)

questions.q: According to Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences, ___ intelligence is about self-knowledge and the ability to act adaptively on the basis of that knowledge
questions.explanation: Lecture: "intrapersonal ... the self-knowledge ... ability to act adaptively". (Lecture 8)

questions.q: In the PASS theory of intelligence, PASS stands for ___
questions.explanation: "PASS model ... planning, attention, simultaneous and successive processing" (Das). (Lecture 9)

questions.q: Pre-assessment, group based initial instruction, regular formative assessments, corrective instruction, and parallel formative assessments are all components of ___
questions.explanation: Mastery learning: pre-assessment, instruction, formative assessment, "corrective instruction, parallel formative assessments" and enrichment. (Lecture 10)

questions.q: Which of the following is an approach to learning which suggests that reality is determined by the experiences of the learner?
questions.explanation: Constructivism: every learner constructs their own knowledge from experience. (Lecture 10)

questions.q: ___ constructivism is based on the work of Lev Vygotsky.
questions.explanation: "social constructivism ... Lev Vygotsky is the propagator". (Lecture 10)

questions.q: Which of the following is not a stage of development as given by Piaget?
questions.explanation: Piaget's four stages: sensory-motor, pre-operational, concrete operational, formal operational. (Lecture 10)

questions.q: According to Vygotsky, ___ is the gap between what a learner can do independently and what they can do with the help of a more knowledgeable other.
questions.explanation: Vygotsky "has defined ... the zone of proximal development". (Lecture 10)

questions.q: ___ teaching involves an interactive dialogue between a teacher and a small group of students.
questions.explanation: "reciprocal teaching ... having an interactive dialogue between the teacher and the small groups" (Lecture 10)

questions.q: Researchers have long believed that memories form due to changes in the brain ___
questions.explanation: Memory forms through changes in connections between nerve cells (neurons/synapses); only "neurons" fits. (Lecture 11: Memory & Cognition)

questions.q: ___ refers to calling back the stored information in response to some cue for use in a process or activity
questions.explanation: "the next process is the retrieval, recall or recollection" when information is needed in response to cues. (Lecture 11: Memory & Cognition)

questions.q: The duration of the sensory register is ___
questions.explanation: Sensory register: "the duration is one to three seconds". (Lecture 12)

questions.q: Maintenance rehearsal in the context of short term memory is also known as ___
questions.explanation: Maintenance rehearsal = rote repetition (lecture 12 contrasts rote rehearsal with elaborative rehearsal).

questions.q: Which of the following is not a component of the working memory model?
questions.explanation: Baddeley model: central executive, phonological loop, visuo-spatial sketchpad, episodic buffer; no "language repository". (Lecture 13)

questions.q: ___ describes our implicit knowledge of tasks that usually do not require conscious recall to perform them
questions.explanation: Procedural knowledge/memory = know-how of performing tasks, implicit. (Lecture 14)

questions.q: The Levels of Processing theory in memory is given by -
questions.explanation: Levels of processing (shallow structural vs deep) = Craik & Lockhart. (Lecture 14)

questions.q: ___ processing is when we encode only the physical qualities of something.
questions.explanation: "shallow processing is the structural encoding ... emphasizes the physical structure of the stimulus". (Lecture 14)

questions.q: ___ refers to the cognitive capacity actually allocated to the task.
questions.explanation: "mental effort actually refers to the cognitive capacity actually allocated to the task"; mental load is imposed by the task. (Lecture 15)

questions.q: Which of the following is not a helpful way of improving memory?
questions.explanation: Writing down, repetition, imagery and meaning help memory; over-exertion does not.

questions.q: When there are many possible answers to a solution, we rely on ___ to help us choose the best solution, like trying to answer or solve an open-ended question
questions.explanation: "diversion [divergent] thinking ... multiple solutions to a question which is probably open-ended question". (Lecture 16: Thinking & Cognition)

questions.q: ___ are representative items within each concept.
questions.explanation: Prototype = representative example of a concept (Himalayan mountains example). (Lecture 16: Thinking & Cognition)

questions.q: Cognitive, affective, and psychomotor are three learning domains as given by -
questions.explanation: Bloom's taxonomy domains: cognitive, affective, psychomotor. (Lecture 17)

questions.q: ___ knowledge defines knowledge about own knowledge or self-knowledge
questions.explanation: Types of knowledge: factual, conceptual, procedural, metacognitive (knowledge of one's own cognition). (Lecture 17)

questions.q: ___ is the ability to collect and analyze information to come to a conclusion.
questions.explanation: "critical thinking ... is the ability to collect and analyze the information to come to a conclusion". (Lecture 18)

questions.q: 'Think out of the box' refers to which of the following?
questions.explanation: Creative thinking = going beyond the boundary, new ideas ("think out of the box"). (Lecture 19)

questions.q: Which of the following is not a stage of the creative thinking process?
questions.explanation: Stages: preparation, incubation, insight, evaluation, elaboration; "information" is not a stage. (Lecture 19)

questions.q: ___ is a method of problem solving in which possible solutions are tried until one is successful.
questions.explanation: Trial and error: trying again and again until success. (Lecture 19)

questions.q: In the traditional approach to learning, a student's role is ___
questions.explanation: Traditional (teacher-centred) approach treats the student as a passive recipient.

questions.q: ___ are versatile graphic organizers that can represent many different forms of relationships between concepts.
questions.explanation: "mental maps or versatile graphic organizers ... which can represent many different forms of relationship between the concepts"; mental map = cognitive map. (Lecture 20)

questions.q: Which of the following is not a major component of motivation?
questions.explanation: L21 (Motivation of Learning) lists major components as activation, persistence, intensity (and direction); confusion is not one.

questions.q: ___ refers to doing something or behaving well because one feels an internal pressure to do so.
questions.explanation: L21: introjected regulation = 'doing something or behave well because one feels pressure within'.

questions.q: ___ drives are often referred to as 'tertiary drives'.
questions.explanation: L22: 'the social drives are found as the tertiary drives'; slide 'Types of Drive' biological=primary, psychological=secondary.

questions.q: Incentive theory of motivation is based on the concept of ___
questions.explanation: L22 slide: 'Incentive theory... is based on the idea of operant conditioning'.

questions.q: The Yerkes Dodson law gives a relationship between ___ and ___
questions.explanation: L22: Yerkes-Dodson law plots level of arousal (x-axis) against performance (y-axis).

questions.q: The letter 'M' in the acronym 'SMART' used in the context of goal setting stands for -
questions.explanation: L23: SMART goals - specific, measurable ('can be measured, evaluated'), achievable/assignable, realistic, time-based.

questions.q: Maslow's need hierarchy has ___ number of stages.
questions.explanation: L24: Maslow's hierarchy 'is the five tier model... five layers'.

questions.q: What are the three psychological needs highlighted by the self determination theory?
questions.explanation: L24: self-determination theory's three psychological needs are 'autonomy, competence, relatedness' (Ryan & Deci 2000).

questions.q: Which of the following is not an example of esteem needs in the context of Maslow's hierarchy?
questions.explanation: L24: esteem needs = prestige, accomplishment, achievement; sleep is a physiological (basic) need.

questions.q: Achievement motivation stems from two needs: need to achieve and need to ___
questions.explanation: L25 slide: achievement motivation - 'motive to achieve' and 'the motive to avoid failure'.

questions.q: Who among the following is given major credit for the popularization of the term 'Emotional Intelligence'?
questions.explanation: L26 slide: 'Psychologist Dr. Daniel Goleman popularized the term in his 1995 book'.

questions.q: Which of the following is not a component of emotional intelligence?
questions.explanation: L26 slide: Goleman's five areas are self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, social skills; knowledge is not one.

questions.q: ___ refers to the ability of putting words to feelings.
questions.explanation: L26: identifying and putting words to what we feel 'is called the emotional literacy'.

questions.q: The following are signs of emotional intelligence, except
options: The ability to let go of mistakes
Feelings of empathy and concern for others
An awareness of personal strengths and limitations
Not taking responsibility for one's mistakes
questions.explanation: L26/L27: EI signs include accepting responsibility for mistakes and moving on; not taking responsibility is not a sign.

questions.q: According to Hochschild, the ___ are attempts by organizations to control employees' inner lives or thoughts and feelings; e.g. in the case of flight attendants.
questions.explanation: L29: 'some organizations... have the feeling rules to control the employees' inner lives and thoughts and feelings' (flight attendants example).

questions.q: ___ occurs when someone's emotions and related behaviors lead to similar emotions and behaviors in others.
questions.explanation: L29: emotional contagion occurs when someone's emotions/behaviours lead to similar emotions/behaviours in others.

questions.q: The biological explanation of emotional contagion can be through the existence of ___
questions.explanation: L29: mimicry 'comes naturally... based on the existence of mirror neurons'.

questions.q: Which of the following is not one of three main areas of general creativity?
questions.explanation: L30 slide: 'EC is considered to be one of three main areas of general creativity, together with nonverbal and verbal creativity and creativity in problem solving'.

questions.q: 'A breakup gives rise to song lyrics' is an example of how ___
questions.explanation: L30 slide: 'Emotions can inspire creativity - such as when a breakup gives rise to song lyrics'.

questions.q: Which of the following is false?
options: Emotional intelligence can predict academic performance and workplace success
Meditation or journal keeping can be effective strategies to improve self-awareness
Emotional intelligence cannot be learnt or improved through training; it is genetic.
Improving communication skills aids in improving conflict resolution.
questions.explanation: L28 slide: 'EI can be developed at any stage of life through self-effort & training', so 'cannot be learnt; genetic' is false.

questions.q: Which of the following is not a component of Benjamin S. Bloom's taxonomy of educational objectives?
questions.explanation: L31: Bloom's taxonomy domains are cognitive, affective, psychomotor.

questions.q: Which of the following is not included in the major schools of learning theories?
questions.explanation: L31: schools are behaviorist, cognitive, humanistic, social & situational, constructivist/social-constructivist; biological/evolutionary not listed.

questions.q: Which of the following affect learning?
questions.explanation: L32: factors affecting learning are individual, task and environmental variables.

questions.q: Which of the following is not a task variable?
questions.explanation: L32: task variables = objectives, trainer's competence, variety, communication gap, rationality, task overload; learning capabilities is an individual variable.

questions.q: ___ learning refers to learning that gets students to learn through doing; such as experimentation and play
questions.explanation: L32: 'Active learning... directs the students to learn through doing... experimentation, learning by playing'.

questions.q: ___ learners favor educational lessons that include peer work or participation.
questions.explanation: L32: 'social and linguistic learners... favor the educational lessons that include the peer work, participation, group learning'.

questions.q: Which of the following is not true for effective instruction?
options: It incorporates components of core curriculum
It is independent of the success of the learning experience
questions.explanation: L33: effective instruction 'is directly related to the success of the learning experiences', so 'independent of' is false.

questions.q: The following are principles of instruction given by Merrill, except ___
questions.explanation: L33: Merrill's principles - problem-centred, activation, demonstration, application, integration; no 'formation'.

questions.q: Which of the following is a principle of Instructional Systems Design (ISD)?
options: It should move at an efficient pace
It should keep information outside of context
It should be independent of the community
It should create opportunities for learners to replicate past work and output
questions.explanation: L33: ISD principles - 'should be able to teach the subject matter efficiently'; other options contradict the principles.

questions.q: According to Ausubel, ___ occurs when new information is integrated into existing knowledge structures, also known as mental schemas.
questions.explanation: L34: Ausubel - 'meaningful learning... takes place when the information is integrated into the existing knowledge structure'.

questions.q: Which of the following is not a pedagogical approach in teaching?
questions.explanation: L36 slide: five pedagogical approaches - constructivist, collaborative, inquiry-based, integrative, reflective; no 'refractive'.

questions.q: Constructivism with respect to learning suggests that ___
options: the role of learners is passive
learners are the makers of meaning and knowledge
facilitators are the makers of meaning and knowledge
internet is the maker of meaning and knowledge
questions.explanation: L36: constructivist approach - 'Learners are the makers of the meaning and knowledge'.

questions.q: Which of the following is false about pedagogy in education and learning?
options: Effective pedagogies are an amalgamation of various teaching techniques
Pedagogy is based on a facilitator-centered approach
Pedagogy allows teachers to evaluate individual students' performance regularly
Pedagogy allows students to meet like-minded people and learn from their peers
questions.explanation: L37 slide: 'Pedagogy is based on a student-centered approach'; the other three statements are on the same slide, so the facilitator-centred option is the false one.

questions.q: Which of the following is not a major component of the experiential learning process?
questions.explanation: L37 slide: experiential learning cycle - experiencing, sharing, processing/analyzing, generalizing, application; no 'overthinking'.

questions.q: David Kolb's experiential learning style theory typically suggests ___ number of stages in the experiential learning cycle.
questions.explanation: L37: Kolb's model 'has the four stage of learning cycle'.

questions.q: The stages of the experiential learning cycle given by Kolb are dissected by two continuums relating to perception and ___
questions.explanation: L37: 'these are two continuums... how do we perceive... and how do we process' (perception and processing continuums).

questions.q: The ___ learning style as given by Kolb suggests that these individuals prefer technical tasks and like to be left alone to solve them.
questions.explanation: L37: converging style - 'prefer technical tasks... would like to be left alone to solve them'.

questions.q: The model of multimedia learning is based upon some primary assumptions as given by Mayer that are mentioned below. Which of the following is false?
options: Visual and auditory experiences/information are processed through separate and distinct information processing 'channels'
Each information processing channel is limited in its ability to process experience/information
Processing experience/information in channels is an active cognitive process designed to construct coherent mental representations
questions.explanation: L38: Mayer's assumptions - two separate channels, each limited in capacity, processing is an active cognitive process; all true, so none is false.

questions.q: The ___ principle of multimedia learning suggests that students learn better when corresponding words and pictures are presented simultaneously rather than successively
questions.explanation: L38: 'temporal contiguity principle says the students learn better when corresponding words and the pictures are presented simultaneously rather than successively'.

questions.q: Mezirow(1978) identified ___ number of steps that are required for transformative learning to occur.
questions.explanation: L39: Mezirow 'has suggested the 10 steps for transformative learning to occur, first thing is the disorienting dilemma'.

questions.q: Which of the following is not a feature of e-learning?
questions.explanation: L41 (Psychology of E-Learning) lists features: accessibility, user friendliness, social justice, personalization, individualization, learner-centredness, open/lifelong learning; 'stereotypical' is not one.

questions.q: Many students in the context of a digital classroom regard knowledge of ___ as more important than 'what'.
questions.explanation: L41 slide: 'Many students regard knowledge of how to as more important than what'.

questions.q: Which of the following is not a benefit of e-learning?
questions.explanation: Corrected after checking the lecture (was: None of the above). L41-42 slides list benefits: accommodates everyone's needs, lectures multiple times, scalability, quick delivery ('learners can determine their own speed'), consistency, reduced costs, environment-friendly; not 'motivating' - the L42 slide instead says 'Learners are required to keep themselves motivated'.

questions.q: When we are learning or practicing something, our brain ___
options: builds strong connections between the muscles and bones
questions.explanation: L42 slide: 'When we're learning, our brain makes new connections between neurons.'

questions.q: The ___ theory suggests that when we overload our working memory, we are unable to acquire and process new information.
questions.explanation: L43: overloading limited-capacity working memory during e-learning 'creates a cognitive load ... cognitive overload takes place'.

questions.q: The brain often benefits from physically writing in a notebook since it contributes to ___. Learners during e-learning are hence often advised to take notes.
questions.explanation: L43: writing notes while attending 'enhances the encoding process ... expedite our encoding processes'.

questions.q: In the context of virtual learning, ___ refers to the speed and ease with which a novice user can achieve proficiency with the system.
questions.explanation: L43: 'learnability ... refers to the speed and ease with which the novice user can achieve the proficiency' with the system.

questions.q: Which of the following is not a critical factor that impacts e-learning?
questions.explanation: L43/L44: five critical aspects of successful e-learning are motivation, emotion, self-discipline, social skills, stress; genes are not one.

questions.q: In the context of instructional design, ___ refers to learners' automatic performance on specific procedures with predetermined steps to be followed.
questions.explanation: L44 slide: 'Chaining is referring to learners' automatic performance on specific procedures...'.

questions.q: ___ provides the context to learners in the form of simulated job-related situations where learners have to judge a situation, use the information they have at hand, and make the best possible choice to solve the problem.
questions.explanation: L45: instructional strategies for rapid e-learning - immersive learning 'through simulation, job related situations' (scenario-based), then guided learning, exploration; definition matches scenario-based e-learning.

questions.q: Which of the following is not an essential skill needed for today's teacher (post pandemic era)
questions.explanation: L46: teacher skills listed - digital skills, life skills, communication, creativity, participatory education, inclusive education; non-inclusive education is not one.

questions.q: The following psychological principles about how students think and learn are true except
options: Students' cognitive development and learning is not limited by the general stages of development
Students existing knowledge is not related to and does not impact their present learning
The beliefs or perceptions students have about their intelligence and ability affect their learning and cognitive functioning
questions.explanation: L46 principles: belief about intelligence affects learning; 'what students already know affect their learning'; development 'not limited by the general stages'; learning is context based.

questions.q: Which of the following is true regarding the social and emotional learning of students?
options: Learning is situated in a single isolated social context
Interpersonal relationships are unimportant for development of students
Emotional well-being impacts students' educational performance
questions.explanation: L47 principle 15: 'emotional well-being influences the educational performance, learning and development'.

questions.q: Learners who have a ___ believe that intelligence is malleable and success is related to effort level
questions.explanation: L48: 'growth mindset ... the intelligence is malleable and success is related to effort level'.

questions.q: Acquiring long-term knowledge and skill is largely dependent on ___
questions.explanation: L46: 'the acquisition of the knowledge and the skills in the long term depends largely on practice'.

questions.q: Use of ___ goals increase self-efficacy and competency towards larger goals.
questions.explanation: L47 slide (Principle 12): short-term (proximal), specific, challenging objectives are more motivating; L48 links proximal goals to self-efficacy and competency.

questions.q: The following are examples of formative assessment except ___
questions.explanation: L49 slide: types of formative evaluation - anecdotal records, quizzes, essays, lab reports, diagnostics; entrance exams are listed under summative evaluation.

questions.q: Summative assessment is conducted ___
questions.explanation: L49: summative assessment is at the end of the unit/semester, after instruction.

questions.q: Which of the following is not an appropriate principle of good feedback practice?
options: Provides opportunities to close the gap between current and desired performance
Helps clarify what good performance is
Provides information to teachers that can be used to help shape the teaching
Encourages positive motivational beliefs and self-esteem
questions.explanation: L50 seven principles of good feedback practice: facilitates self-assessment/reflection, clarifies good performance, closes the gap, encourages motivational beliefs and self-esteem, informs teaching.

questions.q: Which of the following is not one of the levels of feedback?
questions.explanation: L50 levels of feedback: task level, process level, personal level; no facilitator level.
